content: Applera Corporation, headquartered in Norwalk, Connecticut, was ranked 874 on the 2007 Fortune 1000 list. It is one of the largest international biotechnology companies in the United States. The company originated as the Life Sciences Division of Perkin-Elmer Corporation. Applera is not publicly traded as a single entity but operates through two major groups with publicly traded tracking stocks in the proteomics industrial sector. These groups are the S&P 500-listed Applera Corp Applied Biosystems Group, based in Foster City, California, and Applera Corp Celera Genomics Group, based in Rockville, Maryland. The company’s history dates back to 1931 under Perkin-Elmer, but its modern form began in 1999 when Perkin-Elmer split its business. The traditional half of the business was sold to EG&G Inc., along with the Perkin-Elmer name, which was more closely associated with the traditional product line. EG&G subsequently became the new PerkinElmer. The remaining Connecticut-based Life Sciences company issued two tracking stocks and renamed itself PE Corporation. The Applied Biosystems group was initially renamed PE Biosystems but reverted to the Applied Biosystems name in 2000, with the stock ticker symbol ABI. PE Corporation was renamed Applera, a combination of the names Applied and Celera. The Applera Corporation Board of Directors oversees the parent corporation and the operations of both tracking stock groups. They are responsible for balancing the interests of investors in both groups. Notable directors include Joseph F. (retired Chairman and CEO of Sea-Land Corporation), Robert H. (Harvard Business School professor), Carolyn W. (Sterling Professor at Yale School of Medicine), and Tony L. White (Chairman, President, and CEO of Applera Corporation). The original Perkin-Elmer, and later its successor PE Corporation and Applera Corporation, were headquartered in Norwalk, Connecticut. In the early 1990s, Perkin-Elmer, a manufacturer of diverse electronic instruments and analytical equipment, established strong ties with groups involved in decoding the human genome. By the late 1990s, its Life Sciences division became a central player in the competition against the public consortium working on the Human Genome Project (HGP). This involvement made Perkin-Elmer a prominent name in biotechnology during the decade. Perkin-Elmer transformed into Applera, focusing entirely on life sciences. The U.S. government supported the HGP with funding, aiming to complete human DNA mapping by 2005. Dr. James D. Watson, who founded the public consortium, estimated the project would take 15 years and cost $3 billion. Perkin-Elmer’s Applied Biosystems division developed thermal cyclers and automated sequencers for genomics companies. By 1995, the company had sold its 30,000th thermal cycler and developed mapping kits with markers every 10 million bases along each chromosome to meet HGP goals. DNA fingerprinting using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) became accepted in court as reliable forensic evidence. In 1996, Tony L. White became President and CEO of Perkin-Elmer and reorganized it into two divisions: Analytical Instruments and PE Applied Biosystems. The latter accounted for half of the company’s revenue, with net revenues increasing by 26%. In 1998, Perkin-Elmer acquired PerSeptive Biosystems, a leader in biomolecule purification systems for protein analysis. This acquisition led to the formation of the PE Biosystems division, consolidating Applied Biosystems, PerSeptive Biosystems, Tropix, and PE Informatics. By 1998, PE Biosystems’ president, Michael W. Hunkapiller, calculated that private industry could decode the human genome before the academic consortium, at a fraction of the cost. This bold prediction led to the creation of the Celera Genomics Group in Rockville, Maryland, with the goal of sequencing the human genome by 2001. Dr. J. Craig Venter, a pioneer in genomic research, became President and Chief Scientific Officer of Celera. The group used the ABI PRISM® 3700 DNA Analyzer, a revolutionary machine developed with Hitachi, Ltd., capable of decoding vast amounts of genetic material in a single day. In 1999, Perkin-Elmer Corporation reorganized into PE Corporation, issuing two new tracking stocks for its Life Sciences groups: PE Biosystems Group and Celera Genomics Group. The reorganization was completed in May 1999, and the two new stocks began trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Later that year, Dr. Afeyan, who oversaw the creation of the Celera tracking stock, left to co-found Flagship Ventures. In 2000, PE Corporation changed its name to Applera Corporation, and PE Biosystems Group became Applied Biosystems Group, with the ticker symbol ABI. Celera Genomics made headlines that year by completing the sequencing and first assembly of the human genome and the fruit fly genome. However, in 2002, Celera shifted its focus from gene discovery to pharmaceutical development, leading to the departure of Dr. Venter, who lacked experience in drug development. By 2004, Applied Biosystems Group’s long-term president, Mike Hunkapiller, retired and was succeeded by Cathy Burzik. Applera Corporation continued to evolve, with Applied Biosystems focusing on marketing its instruments and databases, while Celera pursued pharmaceutical drug development.
